A carrel is a small, private study space designed for one person to sit, read, and work quietly — and it is found almost exclusively inside libraries.

Think of a carrel as a personal little nook carved out within a larger library. Its whole purpose is to give a single person a quiet, dedicated spot to concentrate — away from the bustle of open reading rooms and shared tables.

A typical carrel is a compact desk enclosed by partitions on three sides — left, right, and back — with the front open so you can sit down and stand up. These walls block you from seeing, and being seen by, the people around you. The result feels like a mini personal workspace: just you, your books, your notes, and (in modern libraries) perhaps a power outlet and a small lamp.

Some carrels are even more enclosed — essentially a tiny private room with a door, built right inside the library. These are far more private than the partitioned kind, and are usually reserved for specific users (more on that below).

Carrels are most common in academic and research libraries — the kind you find at universities, law schools, medical schools, and large public research institutions. You will rarely, if ever, hear the word "carrel" used outside a library setting. In everyday offices, a similar-looking workspace would be called a cubicle — but a carrel is specifically a library thing, and the word carries that specific meaning.

Carrels serve two kinds of people:

  1. General library visitors — Any student or researcher who walks into a library and wants a quiet, semi-private desk can often sit at an available open carrel. This is no different from claiming a seat, except that the partitions give you more focus and privacy than a shared table.
  2. Assigned, long-term users — Many university libraries assign specific enclosed carrels to graduate students (especially PhD candidates writing a dissertation), researchers, or faculty members for an extended period — sometimes an entire semester or even a year. These assigned carrels function almost like a tiny personal office inside the library. The user gets a key, can leave their books and materials there overnight, and has a guaranteed, permanent workspace close to the library's collections. This kind of carrel is a significant privilege, because it saves the researcher from carrying heavy books back and forth every day.
The Key Qualities That Define a Carrel

• It is small. A carrel fits only one person. There is no concept of a carrel for two.
  • It offers privacy and enclosure. This is what distinguishes it from an ordinary library desk or table. The walls or partitions are essential to its identity.
  • It is inside a library. This is the defining context. The word is bound to the library environment.
  • It is meant for focused, individual work — reading, writing, research — not casual socializing.

If you have ever seen a quiet corner of a library with small desk-booths separated by wooden or glass dividers — each just big enough for one person to sit, open a few books, and spread out some notes — those are carrels. If the library has a separate row of tiny, closet-sized rooms with individual doors along a corridor, those enclosed rooms are also carrels.

The word "carrel" covers both types described above — the open partitioned desk and the enclosed private room — as long as it is inside a library and designed for solitary study. Some people use "carrel" specifically for the partitioned desk type and call the enclosed room a "study room" or "dissertation carrel," but in standard usage, both fall under the single word carrel.

A carrel is a small, enclosed or semi-enclosed, single-person study space — typically a partitioned desk or a tiny private room — found inside a library and designed for quiet, focused, individual work.
